title: Godly Righteousness
overview: Matthew Chapter 6 presents Jesus’ teaching on sincere piety, emphasizing the importance of doing good deeds, praying, and fasting in humility and secrecy rather than for public recognition. It contains the Lord’s Prayer, a model for how believers should communicate with God, highlighting dependence on Him for daily needs and forgiveness. The chapter also contrasts earthly treasures with heavenly ones, urging believers to prioritize spiritual wealth and trust God’s provision. It addresses anxiety about material needs, calling for faith in God’s care. This chapter is central in the Sermon on the Mount, revealing the heart attitude God desires in worship and daily living, and instructing believers on authentic devotion that pleases the Father.
structure:
**Verses 1-4: Giving in Secret.** Jesus warns against performing acts of charity for public acclaim, teaching that true almsgiving is done discreetly so that God, who sees in secret, will reward openly.

**Verses 5-15: Prayer and Forgiveness.** Jesus contrasts hypocritical public prayer with private, sincere communication with God, providing the Lord’s Prayer as a model. He stresses the necessity of forgiving others to receive God’s forgiveness.

**Verses 16-18: Fasting in Humility.** Jesus instructs believers to fast without drawing attention, maintaining a normal appearance so that fasting remains a private act between the believer and God.

**Verses 19-24: Treasures and Priorities.** Jesus teaches about storing treasures in heaven rather than on earth, explaining that one’s heart follows their treasure and warning against serving both God and money.

**Verses 25-34: Trusting God’s Provision.** Jesus encourages believers not to worry about material needs, using birds and lilies as examples of God’s care, and calls them to seek first God’s kingdom and righteousness, trusting all else will be provided.

keyVerses.text: But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly .
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights the importance of private, sincere prayer rather than public display, emphasizing God’s intimate knowledge of our hearts and His reward for genuine devotion.

keyVerses.text: After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.
keyVerses.significance: The Lord’s Prayer provides a foundational pattern for Christian prayer, emphasizing God’s holiness, kingdom, provision, forgiveness, and protection, encapsulating key elements of faith and dependence on God.

keyVerses.text: Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
keyVerses.significance: These verses teach the eternal value of heavenly treasures over earthly possessions, underscoring the spiritual principle that one’s heart follows what they truly value.

keyVerses.text: But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.
keyVerses.significance: This verse encapsulates the chapter’s call to prioritize God’s kingdom and righteousness above all else, promising God’s provision for material needs as a result of faithful trust.

characters.name: Jesus Christ
characters.description: The central teacher and speaker in this chapter, Jesus instructs His followers on genuine righteousness, prayer, fasting, and trust in God, revealing the heart attitude God desires.

characters.name: The Hypocrites
characters.description: Representing those who perform religious acts for public admiration rather than genuine devotion, they serve as a negative example Jesus warns against throughout the chapter.

characters.name: God the Father
characters.description: Portrayed as the omniscient and caring heavenly Father who rewards secret righteousness, knows believers’ needs, and provides for His children’s daily sustenance.

themes.description: The chapter emphasizes worshiping God in secret and with a pure heart rather than for human praise, reflecting the biblical call for authentic devotion.
Jesus teaches believers to trust God for daily needs and not to be anxious, reinforcing God’s providential care as a foundational biblical truth.
Forgiveness is presented as essential for receiving God’s forgiveness, highlighting the relational nature of grace within the Christian life.
Believers are urged to prioritize heavenly treasures over earthly wealth, aligning with the broader biblical narrative of storing up rewards in heaven.

historicalContext: Matthew’s Gospel was written in the late first century AD, primarily for a Jewish-Christian audience familiar with Jewish religious practices. The cultural context includes the Jewish emphasis on almsgiving, prayer, and fasting as key religious duties, often performed publicly in synagogues and marketplaces. The political situation was under Roman occupation, which influenced daily life and religious expression. Public displays of piety were common, but Jesus challenges these norms by teaching that true righteousness is a matter of the heart and relationship with God rather than external show.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology emphasizes the sovereignty of God in providing for His people and the necessity of heartfelt, covenantal obedience. This view highlights the chapter’s call to trust God’s providence and the importance of genuine repentance and forgiveness.

Dispensationalists often see this chapter as part of Jesus’ ethical teachings for the Church age, stressing the distinction between earthly and heavenly priorities and the believer’s responsibility to live a holy life while awaiting Christ’s return.

Early Church Fathers like Augustine interpreted the Lord’s Prayer as a comprehensive guide to Christian life, emphasizing humility, dependence on God, and the spiritual meaning behind fasting and almsgiving as means of sanctification.

crossReferences.connection: Contains a parallel version of the Lord’s Prayer, reinforcing Jesus’ teaching on prayer in Matthew 6.
Paul exhorts believers not to be anxious but to present their requests to God, echoing Jesus’ teaching on trust and prayer.
Warns against the love of money, complementing Jesus’ teaching about serving God rather than mammon.
Encourages believers to confess sins and pray for one another, linking to the theme of forgiveness in Matthew 6.
Invites believers to approach God’s throne of grace with confidence, resonating with the intimate prayer relationship taught in this chapter.

application: Practice giving, praying, and fasting privately to cultivate sincere devotion rather than seeking human approval.
Use the Lord’s Prayer as a daily model to deepen your communication with God and align your heart with His will.
Prioritize spiritual treasures by investing time and resources in God’s kingdom rather than accumulating earthly wealth.
Trust God daily for your needs, releasing anxiety by remembering His faithful provision as demonstrated in creation.
Forgive others genuinely to maintain a right relationship with God and experience His forgiveness in your life.
conclusion: Matthew 6 challenges believers to examine the motives behind their religious practices and to cultivate a faith marked by humility, sincerity, and trust in God’s provision. By teaching the Lord’s Prayer, emphasizing forgiveness, and urging a heavenly perspective on treasures and worries, this chapter provides timeless guidance for living a life pleasing to God. Its call to secret devotion and reliance on God’s care remains foundational for Christian discipleship and spiritual growth today.
timeline: c. AD 30-33 - Ministry of Jesus Christ

definitions.definition: Charitable giving to the poor, considered a religious duty in Jewish tradition.
A private room or space for prayer and meditation, symbolizing secrecy and intimacy with God.
A term used to describe wealth or material riches, often personified as a false master competing with God.
The voluntary abstaining from food for spiritual purposes, often accompanied by prayer and repentance.

outline.heading: Giving in Secret
outline.description: Jesus teaches that acts of charity should be done discreetly, not for public praise, emphasizing God’s reward for secret righteousness.

outline.heading: Prayer and Forgiveness
outline.description: Instructions on private prayer contrasted with hypocritical public prayer, introduction of the Lord’s Prayer, and the necessity of forgiving others.

outline.heading: Fasting in Humility
outline.description: Jesus instructs believers to fast without outward signs of distress, maintaining a normal appearance to keep fasting between the individual and God.

outline.heading: Treasures and Priorities
outline.description: Teaching on storing treasures in heaven rather than on earth, the connection between treasure and the heart, and the impossibility of serving both God and money.

outline.heading: Trusting God’s Provision
outline.description: Encouragement not to worry about material needs, using examples from nature to illustrate God’s care, and a call to seek God’s kingdom first.
